facts.statement: The genus Edmontosaurus includes synonyms such as Anatosaurus, Anatotitan, Claosaurus annectens, and Ugrunaaluk.
facts.quote: synonyms: *AnatosaurusLull & Wright, 1942 AnatotitanChapman & Brett-Surman, 1990 Claosaurus annectens Marsh, 1892 Ugrunaaluk?Mori et al., 2015

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus fossils date from the Late Cretaceous, spanning the Campanian to the end of the Maastrichtian.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Cretaceous (Campanian to end Maastrichtian)

facts.statement: The genus Edmontosaurus was named by Lawrence Lambe in 1917.
facts.quote: authority: Lambe, 1917

facts.statement: Fossils of Edmontosaurus regalis are found in western North America and date to approximately 73 million years ago.
facts.quote: Fossils of E. regalis have been found in rocks of western North America that date from the late Campanian age of the Cretaceous period 73 million years ago

facts.statement: Fossils of Edmontosaurus annectens date to approximately 65.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: while those of E. annectens were found in the same geographic region from rocks dated to the end of the Maastrichtian age, 65.5 million years ago

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus annectens could reach lengths of up to 12 meters and average weights of about 5.6 metric tons.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus included two of the largest hadrosaurid species, with E. annectens measuring up to 12 m in length and weighing around 5.6 MT in average asymptotic body mass

facts.statement: Exceptionally large specimens of Edmontosaurus annectens measured around 15 meters in length and weighed approximately 15.9 metric tons.
facts.quote: The exceptionally large specimens of E. annectens measured around 15 m long and weighed around 15.9 MT

facts.statement: The type species Edmontosaurus regalis was named by Lawrence Lambe in 1917.
facts.quote: The type species, E. regalis, was named by Lawrence Lambe in 1917

facts.statement: The species Edmontosaurus annectens was named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1892.
facts.quote: The best known of these is E. annectens, named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1892

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus was distributed across western North America, from Colorado to the northern slopes of Alaska.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus was widely distributed across western North America, ranging from Colorado to the northern slopes of Alaska

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus was a herbivore capable of moving on both two and four legs.
facts.quote: It was a herbivore that could move on both two legs and four

facts.statement: Research on Edmontosaurus fossils has revealed details about its brain, feeding methods, and injuries including attacks by tyrannosaurs.
facts.quote: including its brain, how it may have fed, and its injuries and pathologies, such as evidence for tyrannosaur attacks on a few specimens

facts.statement: In 2025, Tuinstra et al. detected ancient hydroxyproline in an Edmontosaurus fossil, confirming the presence of original organic material.
facts.quote: In an Edmontosaurus fossil, Tuinstra et al. (2025) made the first clear detection of actual original dinosaur organic material, showing the presence of ancient hydroxyproline

facts.statement: The first well-supported species of Edmontosaurus was originally named Claosaurus annectens by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1892.
facts.quote: The first well-supported species of Edmontosaurus was named in 1892 as Claosaurus annectens by Othniel Charles Marsh

facts.statement: The specimens for Claosaurus annectens were collected in 1891 by John Bell Hatcher from the Lance Formation in Wyoming.
facts.quote: Both were collected in 1891 by John Bell Hatcher from the late Maastrichtian-age Upper Cretaceous Lance Formation of Niobrara County (then part of Converse County), Wyoming

facts.statement: The mummified specimen AMNH 5060 was discovered in 1908 by Charles Hazelius Sternberg and his sons near Lusk, Wyoming.
facts.quote: The first, the "mummified" specimen AMNH 5060, was discovered in 1908 by Charles Hazelius Sternberg and his sons in Lance Formation rocks near Lusk, Wyoming

facts.statement: The assignment of Trachodon selwyni to Edmontosaurus regalis is considered of very doubtful validity by recent reviews.
facts.quote: It was not, instead being designated "of very doubtful validity."

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus is classified as a saurolophine hadrosaurid characterized by smaller, solid crests or fleshy combs rather than large hollow ones.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus is classified as a genus of saurolophine (or hadrosaurine) hadrosaurid, a member of the group of hadrosaurids that lacked large, hollow crests and instead had smaller, solid crests or fleshy combs

facts.statement: The genus Edmontosaurus was named in 1917 by Lawrence Lambe based on partial skeletons discovered in the Horseshoe Canyon Formation.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus itself was coined in 1917 by Lawrence Lambe for two partial skeletons found in the Horseshoe Canyon Formation

facts.statement: Specimen NMC 8399 was discovered in 1912 on the Red Deer River by a Sternberg party.
facts.quote: NMC 8399 was discovered on the Red Deer River in 1912 by a Sternberg party.

facts.statement: Charles Mortram Sternberg named Thespesius saskatchewanensis in 1926 based on specimen NMC 8509, a skull and partial skeleton found on the Wood Mountain plateau in southern Saskatchewan.
facts.quote: In 1926, Charles Mortram Sternberg named Thespesius saskatchewanensis for NMC 8509, which is a skull and partial skeleton from the Wood Mountain plateau of southern Saskatchewan.

facts.statement: Thespesius saskatchewanensis was estimated to be between 7 and 7.3 meters in length at the time of its description.
facts.quote: At the time, T. saskatchewanensis was unusual because of its small size, estimated at 7 to 7.3 m in length.

facts.statement: In 1942, Lull and Wright created the genus Anatosaurus to classify several hadrosaurid species that did not fit well into existing genera.
facts.quote: In 1942, Lull and Wright attempted to resolve the complicated taxonomy of crestless hadrosaurids by naming a new genus, Anatosaurus, to take in several species that did not fit well under their previous genera.

facts.statement: The genus Anatosaurus, meaning 'duck lizard' due to its wide, duck-like beak, was established with Marsh's Claosaurus annectens as its type species.
facts.quote: Anatosaurus, meaning duck lizard, because of its wide, duck-like beak (Latin anas duck + Greek lizard), had as its type species Marsh's old Claosaurus annectens.

facts.statement: Brett-Surman and Ralph Chapman designated the new genus Anatotitan for A. copei in 1990.
facts.quote: Brett-Surman and Ralph Chapman designated a new genus for A. copei (Anatotitan) in 1990.

facts.statement: A specimen nicknamed 'Dakota' was discovered in 1999 by Tyler Lyson in the Hell Creek Formation of North Dakota and was announced in 2007.
facts.quote: In 2007, another "mummy" was announced. Nicknamed "Dakota", it was discovered in 1999 by Tyler Lyson and came from the Hell Creek Formation of North Dakota.

facts.statement: The name Anatosaurus is considered a junior synonym of Edmontosaurus because its type species was reassigned to Edmontosaurus.
facts.quote: Because the type species of Anatosaurus (A. annectens) was sunk into Edmontosaurus, the name Anatosaurus is abandoned as a junior synonym of Edmontosaurus.

facts.statement: A previous conception of Edmontosaurus included three valid species: E. regalis, E. annectens, and E. saskatchewanensis.
facts.quote: The conception of Edmontosaurus that emerged included three valid species: the type species E. regalis, E. annectens (including Anatosaurus edmontoni, amended to edmontonensis), and E. saskatchewanensis.

facts.statement: The proper taxonomy of the A. copei specimens remains a subject of ongoing debate.
facts.quote: The debate about the proper taxonomy of the A. copei specimens continues to the present day.

facts.statement: A 2011 study by Campione and Evans concluded that only two species of Edmontosaurus are valid: E. regalis and E. annectens.
facts.quote: In a 2011 study by Nicolás Campione and David Evans, the authors conducted the first ever morphometric analysis to compare the various specimens assigned to Edmontosaurus. They concluded that only two species are valid: E. regalis, from the late Campanian, and E. annectens, from the late Maastrichtian.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus is currently recognized as having two valid species: E. regalis and E. annectens.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus is currently regarded as having two valid species: the type species E. regalis and E. annectens.

facts.statement: Anatosaurus copei and E. saskatchewanensis are now considered growth stages of E. annectens, with A. copei representing adults and E. saskatchewanensis representing juveniles.
facts.quote: Anatosaurus copei and E. saskatchewanensis are now thought to be growth stages of E. annectens, with A. copei as adults and E. saskatchewanensis as juveniles.

facts.statement: Specimens from the Prince Creek Formation of Alaska formerly assigned to Edmontosaurus were given the name Ugrunaaluk kuukpikensis in 2015.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurine specimens from the Prince Creek Formation of Alaska formerly assigned to Edmontosaurus sp. were given their own genus and species name, Ugrunaaluk kuukpikensis, in 2015.

facts.statement: A 2017 study questioned the identification of Ugrunaaluk as a separate genus, regarding it as a nomen dubium indistinguishable from other Edmontosaurus.
facts.quote: However, the identification of Ugrunaaluk as a separate genus was questioned by a 2017 study from Hai Xing and colleagues, who regarded it as a nomen dubium that was indistinguishable from other Edmontosaurus.

facts.statement: Specimen TMM 41442-1 from the Javelina Formation of Big Bend National Park was initially reported as Edmontosaurus but was later reassigned to Kritosaurus.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus was also reported from the Javelina Formation of Big Bend National Park, western Texas based on TMM 41442-1, but was later referred to Kritosaurus cf. navajovius by Wagner (2001), before being assigned to Kritosaurus sp. by Lehman et al. (2016).

facts.statement: It is debated whether the larger hadrosaurid Anatotitan copei is a synonym of Edmontosaurus annectens rather than a distinct larger species.
facts.quote: Traditionally, E. regalis has been regarded as the largest species, though this was challenged by the hypothesis that the larger hadrosaurid Anatotitan copei is a synonym of Edmontosaurus annectens

facts.statement: Previous estimates suggested that fully grown adults could be 9 to 12 meters long, with some larger specimens reaching 12 to 13 meters and a body mass of about 4 metric tons.
facts.quote: Depending on the species, previous estimates suggested that a fully grown adult could have been 9 - 12 m long and some of the larger specimens reached the range of 12 - 13 m with a body mass on the order of 4 MT

facts.statement: A 2022 study proposed that a fully grown adult Edmontosaurus annectens would measure up to 11 to 12 meters in length and have an average body mass of approximately 5.6 metric tons.
facts.quote: A 2022 study on the osteohistology and growth of E. annectens suggested that previous estimates might have underestimated or overestimated the size of this dinosaur and proposed that a fully grown adult E. annectens would have measured up to 11 - 12 m in length and approximately 5.6 MT in average asymptotic body mass

facts.statement: There is at least one report of a potential Edmontosaurus annectens specimen that is almost 12 meters long.
facts.quote: There is also at least one report of a much larger potential E. annectens specimen that is almost 12 m long

facts.statement: Specimens from the Museum of the Rockies suggest that Edmontosaurus annectens could have reached nearly 15 meters in length and weighed up to 15.87 metric tons, though such large individuals were likely very rare.
facts.quote: Two specimens still under study in the collection of the Museum of the Rockies - a 7.5 m tail labelled as MOR 1142 and another labelled as MOR 1609 - indicate that Edmontosaurus annectens could have grown to much larger sizes and reach nearly 15 m in length, and weighed up to 15.87 MT, but such large individuals were likely very rare

facts.statement: One skull of Edmontosaurus annectens measures 3.87 feet long.
facts.quote: One skull of E. annectens (formerly Anatotitan) measures 3.87 ft long

facts.statement: The skull was roughly triangular in profile and lacked a bony cranial crest.
facts.quote: The skull was roughly triangular in profile, with no bony cranial crest

facts.statement: The beak was toothless, with both the upper and lower beaks extended by keratinous material.
facts.quote: The beak was toothless, and both the upper and lower beaks were extended by keratinous material

facts.statement: Teeth were present only in the maxillae and dentaries.
facts.quote: Teeth were present only in the maxillae (upper cheeks) and dentaries (main bone of the lower jaw)

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus was a hadrosaurid dinosaur known only from the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus was a hadrosaurid (a duck-billed dinosaur), a member of a family of dinosaurs which to date are known only from the Late Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus is classified within the Saurolophinae clade, a group of hadrosaurids that lacked hollow crests.
facts.quote: It is classified within the Saurolophinae (alternately Hadrosaurinae), a clade of hadrosaurids which lacked hollow crests.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus is the namesake genus of the tribe Edmontosaurini, which includes Shantungosaurus, Kerberosaurus, and Laiyangosaurus.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus is the namesake genus of the saurolophine tribe Edmontosaurini, which also includes taxa like Shantungosaurus, Kerberosaurus and Laiyangosaurus.

facts.statement: The genus Edmontosaurus was named by Lambe in 1917.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Lambe, 1917

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Edmontosaurus is Edmontosaurus regalis.
facts.quote: type_species: Edmontosaurus regalis

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus annectens was originally described by Marsh in 1892.
facts.quote: subdivision: Edmontosaurus annectens(Marsh, 1892)

facts.statement: Fossils of E. regalis date from the late Campanian (73 to 70 million years ago), while fossils of E. annectens date from the late Maastrichtian (68 to 66 million years ago).
facts.quote: Se han encontrado fósiles de E. regalis en rocas del oeste de Norteamérica que datan de fines del Campaniano entre 73 a 70 millones de años, mientras que las de E. annectens se encontraron en la misma región geográfica, pero en rocas que datan de finales del Maastrichtiano, entre 68 a 66 millones de años.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus lived alongside Triceratops, Tyrannosaurus, Pachycephalosaurus, and Ankylosaurus shortly before the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus fue uno de los últimos dinosaurios no aviares, y vivió junto a dinosaurios como Triceratops, Tyrannosaurus, Pachycephalosaurus y Ankylosaurus poco antes de la extinción masiva del Cretácico-Paleógeno.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus included some of the largest hadrosaurid species, reaching up to 12 meters in length and weighing around 4 tons.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus incluyó algunas de las especies de hadrosáuridos más grandes, midiendo hasta 12 metros de largo y pesando alrededor de 4 toneladas.

facts.statement: Two fossil specimens housed at the Royal Tyrrell Museum suggest a maximum size of 15 meters and 10 tons for Edmontosaurus annectens.
facts.quote: Existe evidencia en forma de dos especímenes fosilizados alojados en el Museo de las Rocosas para un tamaño máximo aún mayor de 15 metros y un peso de 10 toneladas para Edmontosaurus annectens.

facts.statement: The first Edmontosaurus fossils were discovered in southeastern Alberta, Canada, in the area known as the "Lower Edmonton" of the Horseshoe Canyon Formation.
facts.quote: Los primeros fósiles de Edmontosaurus fueron descubiertos al sureste de Alberta, Canadá, en la zona usualmente llamada "Edmonton inferior" que pertenece a la Formación Cañón Herradura.

facts.statement: The type species E. regalis was named by Lawrence Lambe in 1917, though other species now considered part of Edmontosaurus were named earlier.
facts.quote: La especie tipo, E. regalis, fue nombrada por Lawrence Lambe en 1917, aunque varias otras especies que ahora están consideran en Edmontosaurus fueron nombradas antes.

facts.statement: The most well-known species, E. annectens, was named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1892 as a species of Claosaurus, later known as Trachodon and Anatosaurus annectens.
facts.quote: La más conocida de estas probablemente sea E. annectens, nombrada por Othniel Charles Marsh en 1892; como una especie de Claosaurus, conocida durante muchos años como una especie de Trachodon y más tarde como Anatosaurus annectens.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus was widely distributed in western North America, and fossil distribution suggests it preferred coastal areas and coastal plains.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus se distribuyó ampliamente en el oeste de América del Norte. La distribución de los fósiles de Edmontosaurus sugiere que prefirió las costas y las llanuras costeras.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus was a herbivore capable of moving on two or four legs.
facts.quote: Era un herbívoro que podía moverse en dos y cuatro patas.

facts.statement: Due to evidence of several bone beds, it is believed that Edmontosaurus lived in groups and may have been migratory.
facts.quote: Debido a que se sabe de varios lechos óseos, se cree que Edmontosaurus vivió en grupos y también pudo haber sido migratorio.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus was a large terrestrial herbivore.
facts.quote: As a hadrosaurid, Edmontosaurus was a large terrestrial herbivore.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus could feed from ground level up to approximately 4 meters above.
facts.quote: The animal's feeding range would have been from ground level to around 4 m above.

facts.statement: The interpretation that Edmontosaurus was a filter-feeder like modern ducks has been rejected because its beak furrows resemble those of herbivorous turtles rather than filter-feeding birds.
facts.quote: This interpretation of the beak has been rejected, as the furrows and ridges are more like those of herbivorous turtle beaks than the flexible structures seen in filter-feeding birds.

facts.statement: Williams et al. suggested Edmontosaurus was a grazer rather than a browser based on scratch-dominated microwear textures on its teeth.
facts.quote: Because scratches dominate the microwear texture of the teeth, Williams et al. suggested Edmontosaurus was a grazer instead of a browser, which would be predicted to have fewer scratches due to eating less abrasive materials.

facts.statement: Comparisons of dental microwear textures suggest that the abrasiveness of food consumed by Edmontosaurus was not drastically greater than that of other hadrosaurids.
facts.quote: When compared to the dental microwear textures of other hadrosaurids, however, those of Edmontosaurus do not suggest that the abrasiveness of food items it consumed was drastically greater than what other hadrosaurids consumed.

facts.statement: While Edmontosaurus's status as a saurolophine is not challenged, its exact placement within the clade remains uncertain.
facts.quote: While the status of Edmontosaurus as a saurolophine has not been challenged, its exact placement within the clade is uncertain.

facts.statement: Early phylogenies, such as the 1942 monograph by R. S. Lull and Nelda Wright, placed Edmontosaurus and various Anatosaurus species as one lineage among several "flat-headed" hadrosaur lineages.
facts.quote: Early phylogenies, such as that presented in R. S. Lull and Nelda Wright's influential 1942 monograph, had Edmontosaurus and various species of Anatosaurus (most of which would be later considered as additional species or specimens of Edmontosaurus) as one lineage among several lineages of "flat-headed" hadrosaurs.

facts.statement: A 2007 study by Terry Gates and Scott Sampson found Edmontosaurus remained close to Saurolophus and Prosaurolophus but distant from Gryposaurus, Brachylophosaurus, and Maiasaura.
facts.quote: A 2007 study by Terry Gates and Scott Sampson found broadly similar results, in that Edmontosaurus remained close to Saurolophus and Prosaurolophus and distant from Gryposaurus, Brachylophosaurus, and Maiasaura.

facts.statement: A 2004 review by Jack Horner and colleagues found a different result, placing Edmontosaurus nested between Gryposaurus and "brachylophosaurs" and distant from Saurolophus.
facts.quote: However, the most recent review of Hadrosauridae, by Jack Horner and colleagues (2004), came to a noticeably different result: Edmontosaurus was nested between Gryposaurus and the "brachylophosaurs", and distant from Saurolophus.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus had front legs that were weaker than its hind legs but long enough to support it while standing or moving.
facts.quote: Al igual que otros hadrosaurios, las patas delanteras eran menos fuertes que las traseras, pero igualmente lo suficientemente largas como para ser usadas al estar en pie o en movimiento.

facts.statement: The animal possessed a long laterally flattened tail and a large head with a wide, semispherical duck-like beak filled with small teeth used to crush food.
facts.quote: Poseía una larga cola aplanada lateralmente y en su gran cabeza tenía un amplio pico semiesférico similar al de un pato en su boca llena de pequeños dientes con los que trituraba su alimento.

facts.statement: Adult Edmontosaurus specimens ranged in size from 9 meters to 14 meters in length.
facts.quote: presentando tamaños en adultos que van desde los 9 metros con especímenes de 13 metros, hasta los 14 metros de largo.

facts.statement: The estimated weight of an adult Edmontosaurus was approximately 4 tonnes.
facts.quote: Esto sumado a un peso estimado de aproximadamente 4 toneladas

facts.statement: The type specimen of E. regalis (NMC 2288) is estimated to be between 9 and 12 meters long.
facts.quote: El espécimen tipo de E. regalis, NMC 2288, se estima entre 9 a 12 metros de largo.

facts.statement: The holotype of E. saskatchewanensis, now considered a juvenile of E. annectens, has an estimated total length of 7 to 7.3 meters.
facts.quote: El holotipo de E. saskatchewanensis, hoy considerado un juvenil de E. annectens, es más pequeño aún, con un largo total estimado de 7 a 7,3 metros.

facts.statement: The skull of a fully developed Edmontosaurus measures around 1 meter in length.
facts.quote: El cráneo de un ejemplar completamente desarrollado de Edmontosaurus media alrededor de 1 metro de largo.

facts.statement: A skull of E. annectens, formerly classified as Anatotitan, measures 1.18 meters in length.
facts.quote: Un cráneo de E. annectens, anteriormente Anatotitan, mide 1,18 metros de largo.

facts.statement: The skull was triangular in profile and lacked any bony crest.
facts.quote: El cráneo era triangular visto de perfil, sin ninguna cresta ósea.

facts.statement: The beak had no teeth, and both the upper and lower parts possessed a horny keratinous sheath.
facts.quote: El pico no poseía dientes, y tanto la parte superior y la inferior poseían un pico córneo de queratina

facts.statement: Teeth were located only in the cheeks, on the maxilla in the upper jaw and on the dentary in the lower jaw.
facts.quote: Los dientes solo se encuentran en las mejillas, sobre el hueso maxilar en la parte superior y en el dentario en la inferior.

facts.statement: The teeth grew in columns, with at least six teeth in a single column.
facts.quote: Estos dientes crecían en columnas, con hasta por lo menos seis dientes en una columna

facts.statement: Known column counts for the two species are 51 to 53 columns per maxilla and 48 to 49 per dentary.
facts.quote: Los conteos de columnas conocidas para las dos especies son, 51 a 53 columnas por maxilar y 48 a 49 por dentario

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus lived from the Coniacian to the Maastrichtian, between 89.8 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Coniacian to Maastrichtian (89.8 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus belongs to the subfamily Edmontosaurini.
facts.quote: Parent group: Edmontosaurini

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus is classified in the family Hadrosauridae.
facts.quote: Family: Hadrosauridae

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus is a member of the class Ornithischia.
facts.quote: Class: Ornithischia

facts.statement: A 2026 study of an Edmontosaurus skull from the Hell Creek Formation found a tyrannosaurid tooth embedded in the nasal, interpreted as evidence of a predation attempt resulting in a bite to the snout.
facts.quote: Wyenberg-Henzler & Scannella (2026) study a skull of Edmontosaurus from the Hell Creek Formation (Montana, United States) with a tyrannosaurid tooth embedded in the nasal around the time of death of the hadrosaurid, interpreted as likely resulting from a bite to the snout of Edmontosaurus during a predation attempt.
